content:
The image shows a corn ear with husks peeled back, revealing the interior completely filled with dark blackish-brown, shriveled masses — the normal kernels are entirely absent/replaced. The stalk appears reddish-brown. The husks are dried tan/straw-colored.

Key observations:
- **Affected part**: Ear (entire interior)
- **Color**: Dark black to dark brown shriveled masses throughout
- **Texture**: Crumpled, dried, crumbly material replacing all kernel tissue
- **Pattern**: Complete replacement of ear contents — no normal kernels visible at all

This pattern of the entire ear content being replaced by dark fungal spore masses is the hallmark of **Head_smut** (*Sphacelotheca reiliana*), where the ear (and/or tassel) is converted into a mass of dark teliospores encased in a membrane that tears open at maturity. This is distinct from Common_smut, which produces localized individual galls on some kernels while others remain normal.

The complete replacement of all kernel tissue with dark spore masses, combined with the intact but dried husks, strongly points to Head_smut.
